# A Bibliometric Analysis of Gene-Editing and Stem-Cell Approaches in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Research (2010–2023)

## Abstract
This report presents a bibliometric analysis of 211 unique works investigating gene-editing and stem-cell-based strategies for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The corpus spans 2010–2023 and exhibits a compound annual growth rate of 29.90%, with output peaking at 36 publications in 2022. The field is concentrated in a small core of journals, led by *Neural Regeneration Research* (13 publications), and is driven by prolific authors such as Ludo Van Den Bosch and Siddharthan Chandran (7 publications each). Citation impact is highly skewed: the mean citation count is 46.20, while the median is 21.00, and 12.32% of works remain uncited. Network analyses reveal a tightly integrated intellectual base organized around C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathomechanisms, with conceptual structures dominated by the intersection of genetics, disease modeling, and therapeutic development. The social structure is characterized by dense, multi-institutional collaboration anchored by the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School and the University of Edinburgh. These findings map the rapid evolution of a translational research front where CRISPR-based genome editing and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models converge to address ALS.

## Introduction
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder with a complex genetic architecture. The discovery of disease-causing mutations in genes such as *C9orf72*, *FUS*, *SOD1*, and *TARDBP* has catalyzed the development of gene-targeted therapeutic strategies, including CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing and antisense oligonucleotide approaches. Concurrently, the advent of iPSC technology has enabled the generation of patient-derived motor neurons and glia, providing physiologically relevant platforms for disease modeling and drug screening. The intersection of these two domains—gene editing and stem cell biology—represents a rapidly expanding research front with significant translational potential. However, the structure, growth dynamics, and intellectual organization of this literature have not been systematically characterized. This bibliometric study addresses that gap by mapping the performance, social, conceptual, and intellectual structures of the field using a reproducible, evidence-based framework.

## Methods
The analysis followed the bibliometric workflow outlined by Donthu et al. (2021) [E067] and employed science-mapping techniques benchmarked against bibliometrix [E068] and VOSviewer [E069]. A deterministic, exact deduplication procedure was applied to source records, yielding a canonical corpus of 211 unique works [E001]. Acquisition was verified as complete: the source reported 211 results, and all 211 were successfully retrieved [E002]. Metadata completeness was assessed for ten fields; coverage exceeded 99% for DOI, language, publication date, reference count, source identifier, title, and year, while abstract coverage was 80.57% [E003]. The temporal window was defined by the minimum and maximum non-missing publication years (2010–2023) [E004]. Annual output was whole-counted by publication year, and compound annual growth was calculated over non-zero endpoints [E006]. Bradford’s law of scattering was applied to source productivity after excluding records without a source name [E019]. Citation counts, which are source- and retrieval-date-dependent, were summarized using descriptive statistics [E015][E017]. Network analyses—coauthorship, institution collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and cocitation—were constructed using association-strength normalization and Louvain community detection [E070]. Candidate nodes were selected by minimum occurrence thresholds, and edges were reduced via maximum-spanning forest plus strongest edges per node [E022–E026]. All figures were rendered deterministically from saved analysis outputs [E051–E066].

## Results

### Performance Structure: Growth, Productivity, and Impact
The corpus exhibits a pronounced growth trajectory. From a single publication in 2010, annual output increased to 36 works in 2022 before declining to 30 in 2023, a year that may be incomplete at the time of retrieval [E005][E007]. The compound annual growth rate over the observed non-zero endpoints is 29.90% [E006]. This expansion is not monotonic; year-over-year changes include contractions in 2017 (−5), 2020 (−6), and 2023 (−6), interspersed with surges such as the 13-publication increase in 2018 [E007].

Productivity is concentrated in a small number of sources. Bradford zoning reveals that 14 journals constitute Zone 1, accounting for approximately one-third of all documents, while 69 journals populate Zone 3 [E019]. *Neural Regeneration Research* leads with 13 publications, followed by *International Journal of Molecular Sciences* (9) and *Nature Communications* (8) [E008][E009]. The entire corpus consists of articles; no reviews or systematic reviews were identified in the source-supplied document types [E014].

Citation impact is highly asymmetric. The mean citation count is 46.20, but the median is only 21.00, indicating a right-skewed distribution [E015]. The 90th percentile reaches 133 citations, and the maximum is 386 [E017]. Notably, 26 works (12.32%) have zero source-reported citations [E016]. The most-cited document, “HDAC6 inhibition reverses axonal transport defects in motor neurons derived from FUS-ALS patients” (2017, *Nature Communications*), has accumulated 386 citations [E018][E027]. Other highly cited works include studies on C9orf72-mediated autophagy regulation (297 citations) [E028], RNA-targeting Cas9 for repeat expansion elimination (258 citations) [E018], and STMN2 cryptic splicing correction (256 citations) [E029].

### Social Structure: Authors, Institutions, and Collaboration
Author productivity is led by Ludo Van Den Bosch and Siddharthan Chandran, each with 7 publications, followed by Philip Van Damme (6) and Ammar Al-Chalabi, Bhuvaneish T. Selvaraj, Fen‐Biao Gao, Giles E. Hardingham, and Wenting Guo (5 each) [E010][E011]. The coauthorship network, constructed with a minimum occurrence of 2, contains 60 displayed nodes and 141 edges distributed across 10 Louvain communities [E023]. The largest clusters are anchored by Chandran (Cluster 3, weighted degree 55) and Van Den Bosch (Cluster 1, weighted degree 46), reflecting two major collaborative axes [E023]. The three-field plot confirms that Van Den Bosch and Guo co-publish frequently in *Nature Communications* on ALS-related topics, while Tania F. Gendron bridges *Nature Communications* and *Molecular Neurodegeneration* with work on C9orf72 and trinucleotide repeat expansions [E021].

At the institutional level, the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School leads with 13 publications, followed by Johns Hopkins University, King’s College London, Stanford University, and the University of Edinburgh (8 each) [E012][E013]. The institution collaboration network (71 nodes, 168 edges, 10 clusters) reveals a polycentric structure [E025]. The University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute form a tightly coupled dyad (Cluster 2), while the VIB-KU Leuven Center for Brain & Disease Research anchors a distinct cluster (Cluster 1) that includes strong ties to Stanford University [E025].

### Conceptual Structure: Keywords and Thematic Evolution
Keyword co-occurrence analysis (minimum occurrence 5) yields a network of 72 nodes and 192 edges partitioned into 6 clusters [E026]. The highest-weighted terms are “Biology” (occurrence 195, weighted degree 1902), “Genetics” (156, 1655), “Gene” (152, 1640), “Medicine” (141, 1452), and “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” (102, 1231) [E026]. These high-level terms form the backbone of the conceptual map, with “Biology” and “Genetics” co-located in Cluster 3, while “Medicine” and “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” reside in Cluster 2, indicating a bifurcation between fundamental genetic investigation and clinically oriented research [E026].

Temporal keyword trends reveal that “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” appeared in only 1 document in 2010 but grew to 20 documents in 2022 and 16 in 2023 [E020]. “Disease” followed a similar trajectory, rising from 1 document in 2010 to 18 in 2023 [E020]. The keyword overlay map (Figure 15) indicates that recent research (mean year ~2021.8) concentrates on terms associated with therapeutic development, while earlier work (mean year ~2016.2) clusters around foundational genetic and cell biology concepts [E065]. The density visualization (Figure 16) confirms that “Biology,” “Genetics,” and “Gene” occupy the highest-density regions, representing the most saturated research areas [E066].

### Intellectual Structure: Cocitation and Bibliographic Coupling
The cocitation network (72 nodes, 204 edges, 5 clusters) maps the intellectual foundation of the field [E024]. The most cocited references, identified by OpenAlex identifiers, include works on C9orf72 repeat expansions (weighted degree 853 and 829 in Cluster 4), TDP-43 pathology (weighted degree 703 in Cluster 3), and SOD1-mediated disease mechanisms (weighted degree 683 in Cluster 2) [E024]. These clusters delineate the major genetic and pathological axes around which the citing literature is organized.

Bibliographic coupling, which measures the shared reference profiles of the citing documents, produces a network of 72 nodes and 208 edges across 6 clusters [E022]. The top-coupled documents include “Gene therapy for ALS: A review” (weighted degree 651, Cluster 3), “Gene Therapy in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis” (600, Cluster 2), and “Mouse models of ALS: Past, present and future” (469, Cluster 2) [E022]. These highly coupled works function as integrative hubs, linking the gene therapy, disease modeling, and stem cell subdomains. The sparse construction parameters—requiring a minimum of 5 references per document and at least 2 shared references—ensure that only documents with substantive bibliographic overlap are connected [E022].

## Discussion
The evidence reveals a field in rapid, though uneven, expansion. The 29.90% compound annual growth rate and the peak in 2022 suggest sustained investment in gene-editing and stem-cell approaches for ALS [E006][E005]. However, the year-over-year fluctuations and the decline in 2023 may reflect funding cycles, the maturation of specific subfields, or incomplete indexing of the most recent year [E007].

The concentration of output in a small Bradford core, led by *Neural Regeneration Research*, indicates that the field has a well-defined set of preferred dissemination venues [E019][E009]. The absence of review articles in the source-classified document types is notable and may reflect the source’s classification practices rather than a genuine absence of review content [E014].

The citation distribution underscores the field’s translational orientation. The highly cited works are predominantly empirical studies that established mechanistic links between genetic mutations and cellular phenotypes—such as FUS-mediated axonal transport defects [E027], C9orf72-regulated autophagy [E028], and TDP-43 cryptic splicing [E029]—or demonstrated therapeutic proof-of-concept, including in vivo base editing in SOD1-ALS mice [E030] and CRISPR-mediated genome editing [E034]. The 12.32% uncited rate is consistent with a field that includes recent publications that have not yet accumulated citations [E016].

The social structure is characterized by two dominant collaborative clusters centered on Chandran (Edinburgh) and Van Den Bosch (Leuven), with strong institutional linkages between the University of Edinburgh, the UK Dementia Research Institute, and King’s College London [E023][E025]. The prominence of the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School in raw productivity (13 publications) [E012] is not fully reflected in the collaboration network’s top-weighted nodes, suggesting that its output may be distributed across multiple, less densely interconnected groups.

Conceptually, the keyword networks reveal a field organized around a core genetic vocabulary (“Biology,” “Genetics,” “Gene”) that is increasingly interfacing with disease-specific and therapeutic terminology (“Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis,” “Medicine,” “Disease”) [E026][E020]. The temporal overlay confirms a shift from foundational genetic discovery toward translational applications, a pattern consistent with the maturation of gene-editing technologies and iPSC-based disease modeling platforms [E065].

The intellectual structure, as revealed by cocitation and bibliographic coupling, is anchored by seminal works on C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathobiology [E024]. The bibliographic coupling network further identifies integrative review and model-system papers that serve as connective tissue between the gene therapy, stem cell, and disease mechanism subdomains [E022]. This structural integration suggests that the field is coalescing around a shared knowledge base, even as it diversifies methodologically.

## Limitations
This analysis is subject to several constraints. First, the corpus is limited to 211 works retrieved from a single source at a single point in time; the completeness claim is relative to that source and query [E002]. Second, citation counts are source- and retrieval-date-dependent and do not account for unequal citation windows; recent publications have had less time to accumulate citations [E015][E016]. Third, network centrality measures are descriptive of the constructed networks and parameterization and do not establish causal or substantive importance [E022–E026]. Fourth, keyword frequencies depend on source metadata and synonym normalization, and the final year (2023) may be incomplete [E020]. Fifth, abstract coverage is 80.57%, meaning that 19.43% of works lack abstracts and could not contribute to content-based analyses [E003]. Sixth, document-type labels inherit source classification practices, and the absence of reviews may be an artifact of those practices [E014]. Finally, all content inferences are based on titles and abstracts; full-text inspection was not performed [E027–E050].

## Conclusion
This bibliometric analysis maps a rapidly growing, translationally oriented research field at the intersection of gene editing, stem cell biology, and ALS. The field is characterized by concentrated productivity in a core of specialized journals, a highly skewed citation distribution dominated by mechanistic and therapeutic proof-of-concept studies, and a social structure organized around two major collaborative clusters. Conceptually, the literature is transitioning from foundational genetic discovery toward therapeutic application, while intellectually, it is anchored by seminal works on C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathobiology. These findings provide a structured, evidence-based overview of the field’s architecture and may inform future research strategy, funding priorities, and collaboration design.
